title: Primes & Prime Factorization
coreInsight: Every positive integer greater than 1 decomposes uniquely into prime building blocks.
targetLearnerRealization: Composite numbers can be broken into factors until only prime building blocks remain, and the final prime multiset is the number's multiplicative structure.
learningObjectives: Distinguish prime, composite, and the special number 1 by counting positive divisors.
Build a complete prime factorization by splitting every composite factor.
Explain why different factor-tree paths produce the same prime multiset.
Use exponents to record repeated prime factors and reconstruct the original number.

continuity.openingCallback: Continue splitting a number through exact divisor relationships until no composite factor remains.
closingSeeds: Two prime-factor inventories can be compared for what they share and what is needed to contain both.
Exponent choices generate every divisor of a number.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Different orders of factoring produce different prime factorizations.
A composite number must have many distinct prime factors.

beats.purpose: Create the need for terminal prime factors by comparing two valid splitting paths.
beats.expectedRealization: Different factor-pair choices for 60 can end in the same four prime leaves.
beats.transitionIn: An exact divisor lets a number split into a product. What happens if every factor that can still split must keep going?
beats.transitionOut: Both paths ended with the same collection: 2, 2, 3, and 5.
beats.whyNow: A path-choice puzzle makes uniqueness visible before formal vocabulary.
beats.entryBridge: Follow each product until every remaining factor has no nontrivial factor pair.
beats.exitBridge: Sorting the leaves erases the branch order and exposes the same inventory.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Two splitting paths collapsing into sorted factor tiles.
learnerPrompts: Which leaves can still be split?
What do the two sorted leaf lists contain?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—both complete paths end with 2, 2, 3, and 5.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep splitting 6, 10, 12, and 4; then sort every terminal factor.

visual.ariaLabel: Two factor paths for sixty ending with two, two, three, and five

steps.body: From 6 × 10, split 6 into 2 × 3 and 10 into 2 × 5.
From 12 × 5, split 12 into 3 × 4 and then 4 into 2 × 2.

resolution.takeaway: A complete split ends at the same sorted prime inventory, even when the branches differ.

beats.purpose: Identify why 1 cannot serve as a prime terminal factor.
beats.expectedRealization: A prime has exactly two distinct positive divisors; 1 has only one.
beats.transitionIn: The leaves 2, 3, and 5 resisted further nontrivial splitting. Compare them with 1.
beats.prompt: Which statement correctly classifies 1, 2, and 9 by their positive divisors?

options.text: 1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is prime; 9 is composite.
1 and 2 are prime; 9 is composite.
All three are prime because they are odd or small.
Only 9 is prime.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—1 has one positive divisor, 2 has exactly two, and 9 has three.
beats.incorrectFeedback: List distinct positive divisors: 1 has {1}, 2 has {1,2}, and 9 has {1,3,9}.

steps.body: The two-divisor definition makes 2 prime. The extra divisor 3 makes 9 composite. One has only one divisor, so it fits neither class.

resolution.takeaway: Prime means exactly two distinct positive divisors; 1 is a separate case.

beats.expectedRealization: Branch order changes intermediate factors but not the final multiset of primes.
beats.transitionIn: Return to the two trees for 60 and ignore the order in which branches were opened.
beats.prompt: Why do the two complete trees represent the same multiplicative structure?

options.text: Their sorted prime leaves are both 2, 2, 3, 5, whose product is 60.
They use exactly the same intermediate branches.
Prime factors must appear in the same left-to-right order.
Adding factors of 1 makes every tree equivalent.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the inventory and multiplicities match, even though the routes differ.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiply the terminal leaves in each tree and compare the sorted lists.

visual.ariaLabel: Matching sorted prime tiles from two factor trees

resolution.takeaway: A prime factorization is determined by the final prime multiset, not by the path.

beats.purpose: Name primes, composites, and prime factorization after the terminal structure is visible.
beats.expectedRealization: Prime factorization is the complete product of prime building blocks for an integer greater than one.
beats.transitionIn: The repeated splitting process has stable endpoints and a stable final product.
beats.name: Prime factorization
beats.conciseDefinition: A prime factorization writes an integer greater than 1 as a product containing only prime factors.
beats.memoryHook: Split composites; lock primes; keep every copy.

beats.purpose: Break the false shortcut that odd means prime.
beats.expectedRealization: Parity alone cannot establish primality; an odd number may have an odd factor pair.
beats.transitionIn: Divisibility by 2 quickly detects many composites, but failing that test is not enough to prove prime.
beats.prompt: Which odd number below is composite?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—21 = 3 × 7, so odd does not imply prime.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Try divisibility by 3: add the digits of each choice.

steps.body: The digit sum of 21 is 3, so 3 divides 21. Indeed, 21 = 3 × 7.
A failed divisibility-by-2 test proves only that a number is odd.

resolution.takeaway: Prime requires ruling out every nontrivial factor, not merely the factor 2.

beats.purpose: Connect repeated prime tiles to exponent notation.
beats.expectedRealization: An exponent counts repeated copies of one prime and preserves multiplicity.
beats.transitionIn: The inventory for 72 contains repeated copies. Compress equal tiles without discarding them.
beats.prompt: Since 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, which exponent form records every copy?

options.text: 2³ × 3²
2² × 3³
2³ + 3²

beats.correctFeedback: Right—three copies of 2 and two copies of 3 give 2³ × 3².
beats.incorrectFeedback: The exponent above a prime counts how many copies of that prime are multiplied.

visual.ariaLabel: Three copies of two and two copies of three grouped into exponent counts

steps.body: 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2, while 3² means 3 × 3. Their product is 8 × 9 = 72.

resolution.takeaway: Exponents compress repeated primes; they do not remove multiplicity.

beats.purpose: Apply complete factorization while distinguishing repeated from distinct prime factors.
beats.expectedRealization: The factorization 250 = 2 × 5³ has distinct primes 2 and 5, whose sum is 7.
beats.transitionIn: Carry the splitting tree to 250, locking each prime leaf and retaining repeated copies.
beats.transitionOut: The full inventory is 2, 5, 5, 5, but the two smallest distinct prime factors are 2 and 5.
beats.whyNow: The approved problem cleanly applies the completed factor-tree process and then asks learners to interpret distinct prime factors.
beats.entryBridge: Split 250 by an obvious divisor, continue until every leaf is prime, then distinguish copies from distinct values.
beats.exitBridge: The animation collects the leaves before deduplicating them for the question.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Branching factor tree with prime leaves visually locked.
learnerPrompts: Can the current composite leaf split further?
Which prime values appear, even if one repeats?
What is the requested sum?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the distinct prime factors are 2 and 5, and their sum is 7.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Complete 250 = 2 × 5 × 5 × 5, then list prime values without repeating a value.

steps.body: Since 250 is even, 250 = 2 × 125.
The distinct prime factors are 2 and 5. Their sum is 7.

resolution.takeaway: Keep multiplicity for the factorization, then follow the question's wording about distinct values.

beats.purpose: Show that a composite may have only one distinct prime factor.
beats.expectedRealization: A repeated prime power such as 81 = 3⁴ is composite despite using one distinct prime.
beats.transitionIn: Repeated leaves are not new prime values, but they still change the product.
beats.prompt: Why is 81 composite even though its prime factorization uses only the prime 3?

options.text: 81 = 3⁴, so 3 is a nontrivial divisor.
A composite must use at least two distinct primes.
It cannot be composite because it is odd.
Its factorization is 1 × 81, so 1 is prime.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—one distinct prime can repeat enough times to make a composite.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Expand 3⁴ and look for a divisor between 1 and 81.

steps.body: 81 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. The factor 3 is neither 1 nor 81, so 81 is composite.

resolution.takeaway: Composite describes having a nontrivial factor, not having many distinct prime types.

beats.purpose: Use prime exponents as structural requirements for perfect squares and cubes.
beats.expectedRealization: Complete exponent groups minimally: pairs for a square and triples for a cube.
beats.transitionIn: Exponent counts can reveal exactly which prime tiles are missing from a required grouping pattern.
beats.transitionOut: Completing pairs needs x = 10; completing triples needs y = 75; therefore x + y = 85.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer uses multiplicities as actionable structure rather than merely compressed notation.
beats.entryBridge: Factor 360, then treat each prime exponent independently when completing pairs and triples.
beats.exitBridge: Minimality comes from adding the fewest copies needed in every prime bin.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Prime-factor tiles grouped into exponent bins.
learnerPrompts: What are the exponents in 360?
Which copies complete even exponents?
Which copies complete exponents divisible by 3?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Complete each exponent to the next multiple of 2, then independently to the next multiple of 3.

steps.body: For a square, make every exponent even: multiply by 2 × 5, so x = 10.
For a cube, make every exponent a multiple of 3: multiply by 3 × 5², so y = 75.

resolution.takeaway: Prime exponents turn a product condition into independent completion counts.

beats.transitionIn: Now build a complete inventory without a supplied tree.
beats.transitionOut: Repeated division and a product check agree on 2² × 3 × 7.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks the core procedure independently.
beats.entryBridge: Remove the smallest prime divisor until the quotient is prime.
learnerPrompts: Which smallest prime divides the current quotient?
Are all final factors prime?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide 84 by 2 twice, then factor the remaining 21.

resolution.takeaway: A factorization is complete only when every factor is prime.

beats.expectedRealization: One is neither, 29 is prime, and 39 is composite.
beats.transitionIn: Use divisor counts and a real factor pair, not size or oddness.
beats.transitionOut: The classifications follow from {1}, no divisor for 29, and 39 = 3 × 13.
beats.whyNow: A near item revisits both high-risk classification errors.
beats.entryBridge: Test possible prime divisors only up to the square root when needed.
beats.exitBridge: Oddness alone did not settle either 29 or 39.
learnerPrompts: How many positive divisors does 1 have?
Can any prime at most √29 divide 29?
What factor pair proves 39 composite?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—1 is neither, 29 is prime, and 39 is composite.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use definitions: 1 has one divisor; test 2, 3, and 5 for 29; note 39 = 3 × 13.

steps.body: One has only one positive divisor. For 29, none of 2, 3, or 5 divides it, so it is prime. Since 39 = 3 × 13, 39 is composite.

beats.expectedRealization: Both proposed starts for 90 finish with 2 × 3² × 5.
beats.transitionIn: Compare two beginnings without assuming that different branches create different answers.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item requires completion and comparison rather than routine factoring alone.
beats.entryBridge: Finish 9 × 10 and 15 × 6 separately, then sort their leaves.
beats.exitBridge: The prime multiset, not the intermediate pair, defines the factorization.
learnerPrompts: What prime leaves come from each starting pair?
Do multiplicities match?

resolution.takeaway: Different valid paths converge to one prime inventory.

beats.expectedRealization: Two cubed times five squared equals 200.
beats.transitionIn: Read exponent notation back into repeated prime tiles and rebuild the number.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item checks that exponent compression remains reversible.
beats.entryBridge: Evaluate each prime power before multiplying.
beats.exitBridge: The expanded product contains three 2s and two 5s.
learnerPrompts: How many copies of each prime appear?
What number do they reconstruct?

resolution.takeaway: An exponent inventory uniquely reconstructs its product.

beats.purpose: Assess minimal exponent completion for a perfect square.
beats.expectedRealization: For 540 = 2² × 3³ × 5, multiplying by 3 × 5 = 15 makes all exponents even.
beats.transitionIn: Finish with a new number whose prime bins need two independent repairs.
beats.whyNow: The challenge transfers exponent structure beyond the authentic example.
beats.entryBridge: Factor 540 and add the smallest number of prime copies needed for even exponents.
beats.exitBridge: Every missing copy is necessary; removing either 3 or 5 leaves an odd exponent.
learnerPrompts: Which exponents are odd?
Which prime copies make them even?
Why is the multiplier least?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 540 = 2² × 3³ × 5 and repair only the odd exponents.

steps.body: 540 = 2² × 3³ × 5¹. The exponents of 3 and 5 are odd, so multiply by 3 × 5 = 15.
540 × 15 = 2² × 3⁴ × 5² = 8100 = 90². Each added factor repairs a necessary odd exponent.

resolution.takeaway: A least square multiplier supplies exactly one copy of each prime with an odd exponent.

beats.purpose: Consolidate terminal primes, uniqueness, multiplicity, and classification.
beats.expectedRealization: A complete factorization keeps every prime copy and is independent of the splitting route.
beats.transitionIn: Trees, tiles, and exponent bins now describe one stable multiplicative structure.
beats.prompt: Which statements must a reliable prime factorization satisfy? Select all four.

options.text: Every final factor is prime.
Repeated prime copies are retained.
The factors multiply back to the original number.
Different complete splitting paths produce the same prime multiset.
A factor of 1 may be counted as a prime leaf.

response.feedback: Keep prime endpoints, multiplicity, reconstruction, and path independence.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—those four checks capture completeness and uniqueness.
beats.incorrectFeedback: One is not prime, so it cannot be a terminal prime leaf.

visual.ariaLabel: Four checks for a complete prime factorization

resolution.takeaway: Split to primes, keep every copy, and verify the product.

beats.purpose: Create the need to compare two prime inventories in N3.
beats.expectedRealization: Two numbers have both a shared sub-inventory and a smallest sufficient combined inventory.
beats.transitionIn: Write 24 as 2³ × 3 and 36 as 2² × 3², then line up matching prime columns.
beats.prompt: Which prime tiles can 24 and 36 share, and what is the smallest inventory that contains enough tiles to build either number?
beats.takeaway: Next, the shared inventory will become the GCD and the smallest sufficient inventory will become the LCM.
